---
title: "A desire is not a decision"
date: 2020-09-08
---

A desire and an action are different events. I can want something without doing it. But if I refuse to admit the desire, I lose the chance to choose clearly.

Jealousy, sexual desire, hunger for status, or the urge to avoid difficult work can arrive before I have a theory about them. Then culture and self-image label the feeling good or bad. Shame begins when the feeling conflicts with the person I think I should be.

This does not make every drive wise. Some actions harm others; some harm me. Acceptance is not permission. It is accurate observation: this impulse exists. What happens next remains a decision.

Cultures disagree about which desires deserve shame. That variation suggests that at least some guilt is learned. A more useful question than “Should a good person feel this?” is: “What is this drive asking for, and what would happen if I acted on it?”

A drive seen clearly can be examined. A drive hidden behind a moral story still influences behavior, but without scrutiny. I suspect awareness gives us slightly more control, not by removing the drive, but by separating it from action.
